meanings.note: Spoken feminine singular 'you', spelled with final ي to reflect the Jordanian pronunciation inti.

examples.trans: Are you a new girl here?

meanings.note: Core Levantine question word for 'what?' (شو صار؟) and casual conversation starter ('So, ...').
Everyday Jordanian verb for 'do' or 'make' (بعمل وظيفة 'doing homework', بعملوا مشاكل 'making trouble').

examples.trans: How did you do on the exam?

meanings.note: Everyday Jordanian/Levantine word for 'here' (formal هنا).

examples.trans: Come sit here next to me.

meanings.note: Negates past and b-present verbs (ما إجيت، ما بعرف) and idioms like ما عليكم ('never mind'); after قبل or بدل (قبل ما، بدل ما) it links a verb clause.
The main Levantine verb for 'talk / say / tell', far more common in Amman than تكلم.

examples.trans: Tell me what happened with you.

meanings.note: Spoken Levantine dative base taking pronoun endings: إلي (to me), إلك (to you), إلها (to her), إلنا (for us), إلهم (to them).
Clause-linking particle taking pronoun suffixes directly: إني ('that I'), إنك ('that you').

examples.trans: I thought that I was late.

meanings.note: Past tense linking verb (كنت، كنتي، كان، كنا) and subjunctive تكون / نكون ('to be'); ما كان عندي means 'I didn't have'.

examples.trans: I was at school in the morning.

meanings.note: At school, الحمام refers to the student washroom/restroom.

examples.trans: I went to the washroom during recess.

meanings.note: Form II causative verb (khawwaf) from خاف: خوفتيني ('you startled me'), أخوفك ('scare you').

examples.trans: You honestly startled me when you walked in!
I didn't mean to scare you.

meanings.note: Form II verb (fakkar): فكرت ما في حدا هون ('I thought nobody was here').
Spelled في in casual Levantine writing and negated directly with ما (ما في مكان 'there is no place', ما في حدا 'nobody is here').

examples.trans: There is something important I want to say.
There is no time right now.

meanings.note: Everyday Levantine indefinite person word; ما حدا means 'nobody'.
Conversational pivot word acknowledging what was said before moving on or softening an apology.
A female speaker says آسفة (aasfe) when apologizing.
With pronoun suffixes: ما كان قصدي ('I didn't mean to') and شو قصدك؟ ('what do you mean?').

examples.trans: I swear I didn't mean to upset you.
What do you mean by this question?

meanings.note: Versatile Levantine word meaning 'but' between clauses and 'only / just' inside a clause.
As a focus adverb before a verb, noun, or imperative, بس narrows or softens the statement.

examples.trans: I tried to speak, but she didn't hear me.

meanings.note: Followed directly by a subjunctive verb (بحاول ألطف الجو 'trying to lighten the mood').

examples.trans: I'm trying to understand what happened.
Try to calm down a bit.

meanings.note: Form II verb (lattaf): ألطف الجو ('lighten the tense mood').

examples.trans: She told a joke to lighten the mood.
A kind word softens the atmosphere.

meanings.note: Refers to both weather and the emotional vibe of a room (ألطف الجو 'lighten the mood').

examples.trans: The mood is a bit tense today.
The weather is nice in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Softens adjectives, requests, and verbs (صعبة شوي، ارتحت شوي).

examples.trans: Wait for me a bit by the door.
The test was a little hard.

meanings.note: Indefinite كل يوم means 'every day'; definite اليوم means 'today' (مش بعد اليوم 'not after today').

examples.trans: We see each other every day at school.
Today the weather is very pleasant.

meanings.note: Agrees with its subject: اليوم كان صعب (masc.), الخطة صعبة (fem.).

examples.trans: It was a hard day for us.

meanings.note: Signature Levantine word (pronounced ktiir) used before or after adjectives ('very') and after plural nouns ('many').

examples.trans: I have lots of friends at school.

meanings.note: Takes pronoun endings: علي (on/about me), عليكي (to you, f.), عليها (to her), علينا (on/for us), عليكم (on you, pl.). Often contracts to عـ before الـ.

examples.trans: Count on me in this matter.
They lied about me in front of the teacher.

meanings.note: In the past مع ما (ما عرفت شو أعمل), means 'I didn't know what to do'; b-present بعرف means 'I know'.

examples.trans: I didn't know how to answer the question.

meanings.note: Primary spoken verb for 'see' across the Levant, also used in farewells like أشوفك بكرة! ('See you tomorrow!') and نشوفك! ('See you!').

examples.trans: I saw everything with my own eyes.

meanings.note: Asks about manner or state (كيف كان الفيلم؟ 'how was the movie?', شفت كيف... 'I saw how...').
Singular بنت, definite البنت, plural بنات / البنات ('AlRawabi School for Girls' = مدرسة الروابي للبنات).

examples.trans: She is a very bright girl.
The girls are standing in the courtyard.

meanings.note: Form III verb (daayaq) used for teasing or harassing someone (البنات ضايقوكي 'the girls bothered you').
Followed directly by a subjunctive verb: بيقدر يتحمل ('can endure'), بتقدري تاخدي ('you can take').
Spoken Levantine spells and pronounces classical أخذ with د (تاخدي استراحة 'take a break').
Both a quiet personal breather (تاخدي استراحة) and school recess.

examples.trans: We have recess in the courtyard now.

meanings.note: With بـ, بهدوء means 'quietly / in peace'.

examples.trans: I love the quiet in the morning.

meanings.note: Active participle of خاف, very common in speech for 'feeling scared right now' (كنت خايفة).

examples.trans: I was very scared at the time.

meanings.note: With كنت + b-present (كنت ببكي), describes ongoing crying in the past ('I was crying').

examples.text: ما تبكي، كل إشي رح ينحل.
examples.trans: Don't cry, everything will work out.

meanings.note: Everyday oath used earnestly to swear one is telling the truth (والله ما حكيت إشي) or surprisedly in والله جد؟ ('oh really?').

examples.trans: I swear I'm telling the truth.
Honestly, I'm glad to see you.

meanings.note: Standard Levantine future marker placed before a bare subjunctive verb (رح أخلص، ما رح نسكت).

examples.trans: I'm going to tell the truth.

meanings.note: Before an indefinite singular noun, أي asks 'which?' (أي موضوع؟) or strengthens negation ('not any' -> أي إشي).
Imperative feminine اهدي ('calm down!') and plural اهدوا ('calm down, everyone!').

examples.trans: Calm down a bit and take a breath.
Things calmed down after the argument.

meanings.note: Used with manner phrases like بشكل طبيعي ('in a normal way') or بطبيعتك ('naturally').

examples.trans: I acted calmly in front of everyone.

meanings.note: In تصرفي بطبيعتك, means 'act like your normal self / act naturally'.
Everyday Levantine preposition taking nouns (قدام المديرة) or suffixes (قدامهم 'in front of them').

examples.trans: She stood in front of the whole class.
Act normal in front of them.

meanings.note: Universal expression of thanks in both formal and everyday Arabic.
Placed before a name or title whenever addressing someone directly (يا دينا، يا مس فاتن); natural English usually drops it.
Expresses both physical rest and emotional relief after stress (ارتحت هلأ شوي).

examples.trans: I felt relieved when I talked with you.
Sit down and rest a bit.

meanings.note: High-frequency Levantine word for 'now' (contracted from هاد الوقت).

examples.trans: We have to go to class right now.
I feel a bit relieved now.

meanings.note: Used in farewells (أشوفك بعدين! 'See you later!') and narratives (وبعدين 'and after that').
